part2.intro: Three young people talk about their favourite kind of weather.
part2.question: For each question, choose the correct answer.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Lucas
texts.text: I love snow. We only get it once or twice a year in my town, so when it comes, it feels really special. Last winter my uncle took me skiing in the mountains for the first time. I fell over a lot, but I loved every minute. I don't mind the cold – I just wear lots of jumpers. The only bad thing is that the snow turns to ice and the pavements become dangerous.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Mai
texts.text: Most people hate wet weather, but I love rainy days. I like sitting by the window with a book and listening to the rain. Thunderstorms are my favourite. My little brother is scared of them, but I think the lightning is beautiful. I take photos of storms with my phone and put them on my blog. My mum says I should be a weather presenter on TV one day!

texts.label: C
texts.title: Freya
texts.text: I live near the sea, and windy days are the best. My dad and I go sailing every weekend from April to October, and we need a good wind to go fast. When it's too windy for the boat, we stay on land and I fly my kite on the beach instead. I'm not a fan of hot, sunny weather because I get sunburnt easily. Cloudy days are fine for me!

part3.title: The girl who checks the sky
part3.text:
Every morning at half past seven, thirteen-year-old Ana Silva climbs the stairs to the roof of her school in Bristol. She isn't going there to enjoy the view. She's checking the school's weather station.

"It started two years ago," Ana explains. "My science teacher, Mr Hughes, showed us a video about weather forecasters in one of our lessons. Afterwards I asked him if we could build our own weather station. He said yes – if I could find the money." Ana and her friends sold cakes at the school gate for three months and made enough to buy everything they needed.

Now the station measures the temperature, the rain and the wind every day. Ana writes everything in a notebook and then puts it on the school website. "At first only my parents read it," she laughs. "But now lots of parents check it before they decide what clothes their children should wear!"

The most exciting day was last November, when a big storm hit the city. "The wind was so strong that one of our machines blew off the roof," Ana says. "We found it in the car park the next morning. Luckily, it still worked."

Ana wants to study the weather at university. "People think weather is boring, but it's different every day. Next year we're going to start a weather club for younger students. I hope they'll love clouds and thunderstorms as much as I do."

items.q: How did Ana get the idea for the weather station?
options: She read a book about the weather.
She watched a video at school.
Her parents bought her some equipment.

options: Mr Hughes gave them some money.

options: Parents use it to help them dress their children.

items.q: What happened during the storm last November?
options: Some equipment landed in the car park.

items.q: What is Ana planning to do next year?
options: start a club for younger students

part4.title: What is fog?
part4.text:
Fog is really a cloud that is very {19} to the ground. It forms when warm, wet air becomes cold. When there is thick fog, you often cannot see more than a few metres in {20} of you, so it can be dangerous for drivers and pilots.

Some places are famous for their foggy weather. In San Francisco, in the USA, fog comes in from the sea on many summer mornings. People there have even {21} the fog a name – they call it 'Karl'!

In some dry countries, fog is actually useful. In Chile, people put up large nets in the mountains. When the fog {22} through the nets, small drops of water stay on them. The water then runs down into pipes, and villages can use it for drinking and for their gardens.

Fog usually {23} when the sun comes out and the air gets warmer. So if you wake up on a foggy morning, don't worry – by lunchtime it may be a {24} day!

part7.instruction: Look at the three pictures. Write the story shown in the pictures. Write 35 words or more.

pictures.caption: a family having a picnic on the beach on a sunny day
dark clouds and heavy rain; the family running with their picnic things
the family drinking hot chocolate in a café, with a rainbow outside the window

part7.model: Last Sunday was hot and sunny, so Rosa and her parents went to the beach for a picnic. Suddenly, big dark clouds came and it started to rain very hard. Everyone got wet as they ran to a café. They drank hot chocolate there and watched the storm. Later, they saw a beautiful rainbow.

items.q: What will the weather be like on Saturday?

script.t: Dad, are we still going to the beach on Saturday?
I think so. The forecast says it won't rain this weekend.
Great! Will it be sunny?
Not really. It'll be quite cloudy on Saturday, and very windy too. Sunday will be sunny, but you've got your swimming lesson on Sunday.
Then Saturday's fine. I'll take my kite!

items.q: What did the girl leave on the bus?

script.t: Hana, you're really wet! Where's your umbrella?
I left it on the bus this morning. I only noticed when it started raining.
Oh no. Have you got your gloves and your scarf? It's getting cold.
Yes, they're both in my bag. But I'll need to buy a new umbrella.

items.q: Where are they going to go this afternoon?

script.t: It's so hot today! Shall we go to the outdoor swimming pool?
I went there yesterday and it was full of people. What about a walk in the park?
There aren't many trees there, and it's thirty-two degrees!
OK, then let's go to the museum. It's cool inside, and there's a new exhibition about volcanoes.
Good idea.

items.q: What time does the boy's train leave now?

script.t: Hi Tom, are you on the train yet?
No, Mum. Because of the snow, my train is late. It was at half past two, but now it leaves at three o'clock.
So when will you get here?
At about half past four, I think. Can you meet me at the station?
Of course. Keep warm!

items.q: What does the woman want the boy to wear?

script.t: Where are you going, Leo?
To Grandma's farm. I said I'd help her with the animals.
It rained all night, so the fields will be really wet and muddy. Put your boots on, not your trainers.
OK. But it's warm now, so I don't need my coat.
That's fine. And you don't need your cap either – there's no sun today.

part2.intro: You will hear a teacher talking to students about a trip to a weather centre.
part2.title: Trip to the National Weather Centre

script.t: Good morning, everyone. As you know, Year 8 are going to visit the National Weather Centre next month. We planned to go on Monday the twelfth, but the centre is closed that day, so now we're going on Tuesday the thirteenth. The coach will leave from the school car park at quarter past eight. Please don't be late – last time we waited twenty minutes for some of you! The journey takes about an hour. When we arrive, a guide will show us the computers that they use to make weather forecasts. After that, we'll watch a short film. Last year's group saw a film about snow and ice, but this year it's about storms – how they start and why they're so dangerous. In the afternoon, we'll go outside to measure the wind and the rain, so please bring an umbrella. You won't need sun cream – it's not summer! Lunch is included in the price, so you don't need to bring any food. Finally, we'll meet one of the weather presenters from TV, Kate Barton. That's B-A-R-T-O-N. She's going to answer your questions, so think about what you'd like to ask her.

items.q: Where did the group sleep after the problem?
options: in a hotel by the lake
in a building on a farm

items.q: How did Lily feel during the storm?
What did the group do the next day?

script.t: Hi Lily. How was your camping trip with the Scouts?
Well, it was very different from our plan! We wanted to stay three nights by the lake, but we came home after only one.
Why? Was it too cold?
No, it was quite warm, actually. But on the first night there was a huge thunderstorm. The wind was so strong that it broke two of our tents.
Oh no! Where did you sleep?
Our leader, Mrs Price, phoned a farmer near the campsite. He let us sleep in his barn with the cows! It was a bit smelly, but it was dry.
Ha! Were you frightened during the storm?
My friend Zoe was really scared, but I wasn't. I thought the lightning over the lake was amazing. I was just unhappy because my new sleeping bag got wet.
So what did you do the next day?
It was still raining in the morning, so we couldn't go walking or swimming. The farmer showed us how to make bread in his kitchen instead. That was great fun.
Would you go camping again?
Definitely! But next time I'll check the weather forecast first. What about you? Did you have a good weekend?
Not bad. It was too wet to play tennis, so I stayed at home and watched films.

items.intro: You will hear a weather forecast on the radio.
items.q: What will the weather be like tomorrow afternoon?

script.t: Good morning. It's a foggy start today, so drivers should be careful, but the fog will go by ten o'clock. Tomorrow morning will be cloudy and quite cold, and in the afternoon there'll be heavy rain and strong winds across the whole country. If you want some sunshine, you'll have to wait for the weekend, when it will be warm and sunny again.

items.intro: You will hear two friends talking about a holiday.
items.q: How did the girl feel about the weather on holiday?

script.t: How was your holiday in Scotland?
Beautiful! Everyone told me it rains all the time there, so I packed my raincoat and boots. But we had sunshine every single day – I even got sunburnt! I couldn't believe it.
Lucky you! It rained here all week.

items.intro: You will hear a boy leaving a message for his friend.
items.q: Why is the boy calling?
options: to change the time of a game

script.t: Hi Dan, it's Ravi. The tennis courts are closed today because they're covered in ice, so we can't play this afternoon. Sorry! Let's try again next week when it's warmer. Oh, and you can keep my racket until then – I've got another one.

items.intro: You will hear a teacher talking to her class.
items.q: What does the teacher want the students to do?

script.t: Listen, everyone. It's going to be very hot today – more than thirty degrees. At break time you can still play outside, but please stay under the trees and don't run around too much. And make sure you wear a sun hat. I've got some spare ones here if you forgot yours. I can see you've all brought water bottles, so that's good.

items.intro: You will hear a girl talking to her mother.
items.q: What does the girl want to do today?

script.t: Mum, it's been snowing all night! Look outside!
I know. Do you want to go to the ski centre with Dad? Or sledging in the park?
Not today. It's too windy on the hills. I just want to stay in the garden and make a snowman with Tim.
OK, but come in when you get cold.

part5.intro: You will hear Rosie talking to her dad about her friends' summer holidays. What was the weather like where each friend went?

script.t: So, Rosie, have all your friends come back from their holidays now?
Yes, and I've had messages from all of them. Kim went to Spain. She thought it would be really hot, but she says it was quite cool, and so windy that she couldn't put her umbrella up on the beach!
Oh dear. And Oscar? Didn't he go to Norway?
Yes, to the mountains. He expected it to be cold and cloudy. It wasn't very cold, actually, but guess what – one day it snowed! In July!
Amazing. What about Hannah? She went to London, didn't she?
That's right. She wanted to take photos of the city from the London Eye, but it was foggy all morning and she couldn't see anything. It was quite warm, though.
What a shame. And Duc went to Vietnam to see his grandparents?
Yes. He thought it would be hot, but it was actually quite cool, because it rained every day. He says it was wetter than here!
And Leila?
She went to Egypt. There were no clouds at all – it was forty degrees every day! She had to stay inside the hotel at lunchtime.
Well, we had that terrible storm on our holiday, didn't we?
Don't remind me, Dad! Our tent nearly flew away.
